claim: Eukaryotic ribosome precursors acquire translation competence in the cytoplasm through stepwise release of bound assembly factors and proofreading of their functional centers.
source: Eukaryotic ribosome precursors acquire translation competence in the cytoplasm through stepwise release of bound assembly factors, and proofreading of their functional centers.
evidence: This is a general statement about ribosome maturation that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Pre-60S maturation steps include removal of placeholders Rlp24, Arx1 and Mrt4 that prevent premature loading of the ribosomal protein eL24, the protein-folding machinery at the polypeptide exit tunnel (PET), and the ribosomal stalk, respectively.
source: In case of the pre-60S, these steps include removal of placeholders Rlp24, Arx1 and Mrt4 that prevent premature loading of the ribosomal protein eL24, the protein-folding machinery at the polypeptide exit tunnel (PET), and the ribosomal stalk, respectively.
evidence: This statement describes specific maturation steps and is supported by the experimental work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sequential ATPase and GTPase activities license release factors Rei1 and Yvh1 to trigger Arx1 and Mrt4 removal.
source: Here, we reveal that sequential ATPase and GTPase activities license release factors Rei1 and Yvh1 to trigger Arx1 and Mrt4 removal.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Drg1-ATPase activity removes Rlp24 from the GTPase Nog1 on the pre-60S.
source: Drg1-ATPase activity removes Rlp24 from the GTPase Nog1 on the pre-60S
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The C-terminal tail of Nog1 is extracted from the PET following Drg1-mediated Rlp24 removal.
source: Drg1-ATPase activity removes Rlp24 from the GTPase Nog1 on the pre-60S; consequently, the C-terminal tail of Nog1 is extracted from the PET.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data and structural analysis.

claim: Nog1-CTT extraction from the PET enables Rei1 to probe PET integrity and catalyze Arx1 release.
source: These events enable Rei1 to probe PET integrity and catalyze Arx1 release.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Nog1 eviction from the pre-60S permits peptidyl transferase center maturation.
source: Concomitantly, Nog1 eviction from the pre-60S permits peptidyl transferase center maturation
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Nog1 eviction allows Yvh1 to mediate Mrt4 release for stalk assembly.
source: Concomitantly, Nog1 eviction from the pre-60S permits peptidyl transferase center maturation, and allows Yvh1 to mediate Mrt4 release for stalk assembly.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Nog1 co-ordinates the assembly, maturation and quality control of distant functional centers during ribosome formation.
source: Thus, Nog1 co-ordinates the assembly, maturation and quality control of distant functional centers during ribosome formation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: Eukaryotic ribosome assembly is initiated by production of pre-rRNA in the nucleolus driven by RNA polymerase I.
source: Eukaryotic ribosome assembly is initiated by production of pre-rRNA in the nucleolus that is driven by RNA polymerase I (Peña et al., 2017; Kressler et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The emerging pre-rRNA associates with small subunit (40S)-specific r-proteins, snoRNAs, U3snoRNP, numerous U3 proteins (UTPs) and assembly factors to form a pre-40S.
source: The emerging pre-rRNA associates with small subunit (40S)-specific r-proteins, snoRNAs, U3snoRNP, numerous U3 proteins (UTPs) and assembly factors to form a pre-40S.
evidence: This describes established knowledge about ribosome assembly.

claim: Endonucleolytic cleavage releases the earliest pre-40S, permitting the remaining growing pre-rRNA to recruit large subunit (60S)-specific r-proteins and assembly factors to form a pre-60S.
source: Endonucleolytic cleavage releases the earliest pre-40S, permitting the remaining growing pre-rRNA to recruit large subunit (60S)-specific r-proteins and assembly factors to form a pre-60S.
evidence: This describes established knowledge about ribosome assembly.

claim: Pre-ribosomal particles interact with >200 assembly factors during their journey through the nucleoplasm.
source: On their way through the nucleoplasm, pre-ribosomal particles interact with >200 assembly factors, including >40 energy-consuming AAA-ATPases, ABC-ATPases, GTPases and ATP-dependent RNA helicases.
evidence: This is a statement about the complexity of ribosome assembly based on established knowledge.

claim: Pre-ribosomal particles interact with >40 energy-consuming AAA-ATPases, ABC-ATPases, GTPases and ATP-dependent RNA helicases.
source: On their way through the nucleoplasm, pre-ribosomal particles interact with >200 assembly factors, including >40 energy-consuming AAA-ATPases, ABC-ATPases, GTPases and ATP-dependent RNA helicases.
evidence: This is a statement about the complexity of ribosome assembly based on established knowledge.

claim: Export-competent pre-ribosomes are transported through nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) into the cytoplasm.
source: Export-competent pre-ribosomes are transported through nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) into the cytoplasm, where they undergo maturation and proofreading before acquiring translation competence (Nerurkar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Pre-ribosomes undergo maturation and proofreading in the cytoplasm before acquiring translation competence.
source: Export-competent pre-ribosomes are transported through nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) into the cytoplasm, where they undergo maturation and proofreading before acquiring translation competence (Nerurkar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cytoplasmic maturation steps include the release of assembly factors, transport receptors, pre-rRNA processing steps and the incorporation of remaining r-proteins that are critical for ribosome function.
source: These steps include the release of assembly factors, transport receptors, pre-rRNA processing steps and the incorporation of remaining r-proteins that are critical for ribosome function.
evidence: This describes established knowledge about cytoplasmic ribosome maturation.

claim: Cytoplasmic maturation of an exported pre-60S is initiated by the AAA-ATPase Drg1.
source: Cytoplasmic maturation of an exported pre-60S is initiated by the AAA-ATPase Drg1, which directly binds to and evicts the placeholder ribosomal-like protein Rlp24 from the pre-60S (Pertschy et al., 2007; Kappel et al., 2012; Kressler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Drg1 directly binds to and evicts the placeholder ribosomal-like protein Rlp24 from the pre-60S.
source: Cytoplasmic maturation of an exported pre-60S is initiated by the AAA-ATPase Drg1, which directly binds to and evicts the placeholder ribosomal-like protein Rlp24 from the pre-60S (Pertschy et al., 2007; Kappel et al., 2012; Kressler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Drg1-mediated Rlp24 release is a prerequisite for the release of two GTPases (Nog1 and Nug1), the assembly factor Nsa2, the subunit anti-association factor Tif6, the ribosomal-like protein Mrt4 and the export factors Mex67-Mtr2, Bud20, Arx1 and Nmd3.
source: This step is a prerequisite for the release of two GTPases (Nog1 and Nug1), the assembly factor Nsa2, the subunit anti-association factor Tif6, the ribosomal-like protein Mrt4 and the export factors Mex67-Mtr2, Bud20, Arx1 and Nmd3 (Loibl et al., 2014; Zisser et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Following Rlp24 release, the 60S maturation pathway bifurcates to proofread the polypeptide exit tunnel (PET) and to assemble the ribosomal stalk.
source: Following Rlp24 release, the 60S maturation pathway, via a yet unknown mechanism, bifurcates to proofread the polypeptide exit tunnel (PET) and to assemble the ribosomal stalk (Lo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PET maturation is accomplished through the release of Arx1, an assembly factor that covers the tunnel and prevents the premature loading of the protein-folding chaperone machinery.
source: PET maturation is accomplished through the release of Arx1, an assembly factor that covers the tunnel and prevents the premature loading of the protein-folding chaperone machinery (Bradatsch et al., 2012; Greber et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Arx1 release from the pre-60S requires the cytoplasmic zinc-finger protein Rei1, the DnaJ domain-containing protein Jjj1 and Ssa1/Ssa2 (Hsp70) ATPase activity.
source: Arx1 release from the pre-60S requires the cytoplasmic zinc-finger protein Rei1, the DnaJ domain-containing protein Jjj1 and Ssa1/Ssa2 (Hsp70) ATPase activity (Meyer et al., 2007; Meyer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cryo-EM studies have revealed that Rei1 inserts its C-terminal tail (Rei1-CTT) into the PET.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) studies have revealed that Rei1 inserts its C-terminal tail (Rei1-CTT) into the PET (Greber et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Failure to insert the Rei1-CTT into the tunnel impairs Arx1 release and blocks subsequent pre-60S maturation.
source: Failure to insert the Rei1-CTT into the tunnel impairs Arx1 release, and blocks subsequent pre-60S maturation (Greber et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cryo-EM analyses of a nuclear pre-60S revealed that the C-terminal tail of the GTPase Nog1 (Nog1-CTT) intertwines around Rlp24, makes contact with Arx1 and inserts its end into the PET.
source: Cryo-EM analyses of a nuclear pre-60S revealed that the C-terminal tail of the GTPase Nog1 (Nog1-CTT) intertwines around Rlp24, makes contact with Arx1 and inserts its end into the PET (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: For Rei1-CTT to gain access to the PET, the Nog1-CTT end must be extracted.
source: For Rei1-CTT to gain access to the PET, the Nog1-CTT end must be extracted.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data cited in the manuscript.

claim: The 60S ribosomal stalk is built from a single copy of ribosomal proteins uL10 (Rpp0) and two heterodimers of P1 (Rpp1) and P2 (Rpp2).
source: The stalk is built from a single copy of ribosomal proteins uL10 (Rpp0) and two heterodimers of P1 (Rpp1) and P2 (Rpp2), and plays an essential role by recruiting and activating translation elongation factors.
evidence: This describes established knowledge about ribosomal stalk composition.

claim: The ribosomal stalk plays an essential role by recruiting and activating translation elongation factors.
source: The stalk is built from a single copy of ribosomal proteins uL10 (Rpp0) and two heterodimers of P1 (Rpp1) and P2 (Rpp2), and plays an essential role by recruiting and activating translation elongation factors.
evidence: This describes established knowledge about ribosomal stalk function.

claim: On a mature 60S subunit, the stalk is anchored through the interaction of uL10 with rRNA and uL11 (Rpl12).
source: On a mature 60S subunit, the stalk is anchored through the interaction of uL10 with rRNA and uL11 (Rpl12) (Ben-Shem et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: During nuclear 60S assembly, the ribosomal-like protein Mrt4 functions as a placeholder for uL10.
source: During nuclear 60S assembly, the ribosomal-like protein Mrt4 functions as a placeholder for uL10 (Lo et al., 2009; Kemmler et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mrt4 removal from the pre-60S is triggered by the release factor Yvh1.
source: Mrt4 removal from the pre-60S is triggered by the release factor Yvh1 (Kemmler et al., 2009; Lo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: uL10 can be loaded onto the pre-60S to assemble the stalk only after Mrt4 is released.
source: uL10 can be loaded onto the pre-60S to assemble the stalk only after Mrt4 is released.
evidence: This describes the sequential order of events in stalk assembly based on established knowledge.

claim: The nuclear localized GTPase Nog1 co-enriches with a late pre-60S that contains the export factors Nmd3, Bud20, Mex67-Mtr2 and Arx1.
source: The nuclear localized GTPase Nog1 co-enriches with a late pre-60S that contains the export factors Nmd3, Bud20, Mex67-Mtr2 and Arx1 (Jensen et al., 2003; Kallstrom et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In wild-type (WT) cells, Nog1 is not detected on a cytoplasmic pre-60S purified through tandem-affinity purification (TAP) of Lsg1.
source: In wild-type (WT) cells, Nog1 is not detected on a cytoplasmic pre-60S purified through tandem-affinity purification (TAP) of Lsg1 (Kressler et al., 2008; Altvater et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nog1 mislocalizes to the cytoplasm and accumulates on Lsg1-TAP particles upon impairment of the cytoplasmic AAA-ATPase Drg1 or upon treating yeast cells with the Drg1-inhibitor diazaborine (DIA).
source: However, Nog1 mislocalizes to the cytoplasm, and accumulates on Lsg1-TAP particles upon impairment of the cytoplasmic AAA-ATPase Drg1 or upon treating yeast cells with the Drg1-inhibitor diazaborine (DIA) (Pertschy et al., 2007; Loibl et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nog1 travels to the cytoplasm, where it is released in a Drg1-dependent manner and rapidly recycled back to the nucleus.
source: These data show that Nog1 travels to the cytoplasm, where it is released in a Drg1-dependent manner and rapidly recycled back to the nucleus.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited data.

claim: The Nog1 G-domain exhibits characteristic G1–G5 motifs.
source: The Nog1 G-domain exhibits characteristic G1–G5 motifs (Figure 1A, upper panel)
evidence: This is supported by the figure showing the domain organization.

claim: Dominant-negative mutations have been described within the G1 motif of Lsg1(K349N/R/T).
source: Dominant-negative mutations have been described within the G1 motif of Lsg1(K349N/R/T) (Hedges et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A dominant-negative mutation has been described in the G3 motif of Nug2 (G369A).
source: Dominant-negative mutations have been described within the G1 motif of Lsg1(K349N/R/T) (Hedges et al., 2005) and the G3 motif of Nug2 (G369A) (Bourne et al., 1991; Hedges et al., 2005; Matsuo et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dominant-negative mutations in Lsg1 and Nug2 impair the release of these GTPases from a pre-60S.
source: Dominant-negative mutations have been described within the G1 motif of Lsg1(K349N/R/T) (Hedges et al., 2005) and the G3 motif of Nug2 (G369A) (Bourne et al., 1991; Hedges et al., 2005; Matsuo et al., 2014) that impair the release of these GTPases from a pre-60S.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A G224A mutation in the G3 motif of human Nog1 is dominant negative in mammalian cells and induced pre-rRNA processing and assembly defects.
source: A G224A mutation in the G3 motif of human Nog1, which presumably blocks GTP hydrolysis, was shown to be dominant negative in mammalian cells, and induced pre-rRNA processing and assembly defects (Lapik et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: NOG1-G223A (NOG1DN) is dominant negative in yeast.
source: NOG1-G223A (NOG1DN) is dominant negative. Wild-type cells were transformed with a plasmid encoding NOG1 or NOG1DN under control of the galactose-inducible GAL1 promoter and spotted in 10-fold dilutions on glucose- or galactose-containing media.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth assay shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of Nog1DN in galactose-containing medium was lethal to yeast cells.
source: By contrast, expression of Nog1DN in galactose-containing medium was lethal to yeast cells (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth assay shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Nog1DN mutant protein accumulates on the Lsg1-TAP particle.
source: Western analyses revealed that Nog1DN mutant protein, but not Nog1, accumulated on the Lsg1-TAP particle (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Nog1 and Nog1DN protein levels are similar in whole cell extracts.
source: Whole cell extracts (WCE) revealed similar Nog1 and Nog1DN protein levels (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Nog1DN-GFP shows an increase in cytoplasmic signal.
source: Moreover, the Nog1DN-GFP fusion showed an increase in cytoplasmic signal, supporting the notion that Nog1DN release from the pre-60S in the cytoplasm is impaired (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A functional G-domain is essential to evict Nog1 from the pre-60S in the cytoplasm.
source: We conclude that a functional G-domain is essential to evict Nog1 from the pre-60S in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The proteomic heat map obtained using SWATH-MS was in agreement with that generated through SRM-MS and Western analyses.
source: We found that the proteomic heat map obtained using SWATH-MS was in agreement with that generated through SRM-MS (Altvater et al., 2012) and Western analyses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of different analytical methods.

claim: SWATH-MS permitted the quantitation of the approximate residence time of nearly all assembly factors along the 60S maturation pathway.
source: In contrast to SRM-MS, SWATH-MS permitted the quantitation of the approximate residence time of nearly all assembly factors along the 60S maturation pathway (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the heat map in Figure 2.

claim: A Drg1DN:Lsg1-TAP particle accumulated Rlp24, Bud20, Nog1, Mrt4, Nmd3 and Tif6.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Pertschy et al., 2007; Lo et al., 2010; Altvater et al., 2012), a Drg1DN:Lsg1-TAP particle accumulated Rlp24, Bud20, Nog1, Mrt4, Nmd3 and Tif6 (Figure 3A and Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SWATH-MS analysis and is consistent with prior work.

claim: The cytoplasmic chaperone Sqt1 accumulated on the Drg1DN:Lsg1-TAP particle.
source: In addition, the cytoplasmic chaperone Sqt1, which loads uL16 onto the pre-60S (Pausch et al., 2015), and the uncharacterized ribosome-associated factor Tma16 (Fleischer et al., 2006) accumulated on the Drg1DN:Lsg1-TAP particle (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SWATH-MS analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sqt1 loads uL16 onto the pre-60S.
source: In addition, the cytoplasmic chaperone Sqt1, which loads uL16 onto the pre-60S (Pausch et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The uncharacterized ribosome-associated factor Tma16 accumulated on the Drg1DN:Lsg1-TAP particle.
source: In addition, the cytoplasmic chaperone Sqt1, which loads uL16 onto the pre-60S (Pausch et al., 2015), and the uncharacterized ribosome-associated factor Tma16 (Fleischer et al., 2006) accumulated on the Drg1DN:Lsg1-TAP particle (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SWATH-MS analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Lsg1-TAP:Nog1DN particle accumulated Mrt4, Sqt1, Tma16, Nmd3 and Tif6.
source: Like the Drg1DN:Lsg1-TAP particle, the Lsg1-TAP:Nog1DN particle accumulated Mrt4, Sqt1, Tma16, Nmd3 and Tif6 (Figure 3A and Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SWATH-MS analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Rlp24 and its interaction partner Bud20 did not accumulate on the Lsg1-TAP:Nog1DN particle.
source: However, unlike the Drg1DN:Lsg1-TAP particle, Rlp24 and its interaction partner Bud20 did not accumulate on the Lsg1-TAP:Nog1DN particle (Figure 3A and Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SWATH-MS analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both Drg1DN and Nog1DN-trapped Lsg1-TAP particles failed to recruit Yvh1.
source: Both Drg1DN and Nog1DN-trapped Lsg1-TAP particles failed to recruit Yvh1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SWATH-MS and Western analyses.

claim: Rei1 recruitment to the Lsg1-TAP:Drg1DN particle was impaired.
source: Although Rei1 recruitment to the Lsg1-TAP:Drg1DN particle was impaired, Nog1DN-trapped particles recruited Rei1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Nog1DN-trapped particles recruited Rei1.
source: Although Rei1 recruitment to the Lsg1-TAP:Drg1DN particle was impaired, Nog1DN-trapped particles recruited Rei1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Reh1 accumulated on both Drg1DN and Nog1DN-trapped Lsg1-TAP particles.
source: By contrast, Reh1, which functionally overlaps with Rei1 (Parnell and Bass, 2009), accumulated on both Drg1DN and Nog1DN-trapped Lsg1-TAP particles (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SWATH-MS analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Reh1 functionally overlaps with Rei1.
source: By contrast, Reh1, which functionally overlaps with Rei1 (Parnell and Bass, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Nog1DN-expressing cells are impaired in a subset of events along the 60S cytoplasmic maturation pathway.
source: These data suggest that Nog1DN-expressing cells are impaired in a subset of events along the 60S cytoplasmic maturation pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The Nog1-NTD interacts with the assembly factor Nsa2.
source: The Nog1-NTD interacts with the assembly factor Nsa2, whereas the Nog1-G domain contacts the ribosomal-like protein Mrt4, and the Nog1-CTT intertwines around Rlp24 and contacts Arx1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The Nog1-G domain contacts the ribosomal-like protein Mrt4.
source: The Nog1-NTD interacts with the assembly factor Nsa2, whereas the Nog1-G domain contacts the ribosomal-like protein Mrt4, and the Nog1-CTT intertwines around Rlp24 and contacts Arx1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The Nog1-CTT intertwines around Rlp24 and contacts Arx1.
source: The Nog1-NTD interacts with the assembly factor Nsa2, whereas the Nog1-G domain contacts the ribosomal-like protein Mrt4, and the Nog1-CTT intertwines around Rlp24 and contacts Arx1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Nog1, Nsa2, Arx1, Bud20, Mrt4 and Rlp24 are recruited to the pre-60S during nucleolar/nucleoplasmic maturation.
source: Although Nog1, Nsa2, Arx1, Bud20, Mrt4 and Rlp24 are already recruited to the pre-60S during nucleolar/nucleoplasmic maturation, this cluster of assembly factors (Figure 1A) is evicted only in the cytoplasm (Figure 3A) (Pertschy et al., 2007; Lo et al., 2010; Altvater et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nog1, Nsa2, Arx1, Bud20, Mrt4 and Rlp24 are evicted only in the cytoplasm.
source: Although Nog1, Nsa2, Arx1, Bud20, Mrt4 and Rlp24 are already recruited to the pre-60S during nucleolar/nucleoplasmic maturation, this cluster of assembly factors (Figure 1A) is evicted only in the cytoplasm (Figure 3A) (Pertschy et al., 2007; Lo et al., 2010; Altvater et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Release of the ribosomal-like-protein Rlp24 from the pre-60S initiates the cytoplasmic maturation cascade.
source: Release of the ribosomal-like-protein Rlp24 from the pre-60S initiates the cytoplasmic maturation cascade (Figure 3A) (Pertschy et al., 2007; Lo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: On the pre-60S, Rlp24 directly contacts Bud20, and then intertwines around the Nog1-CTT, forming a Nog1-CTT:Rlp24 complex.
source: On the pre-60S, Rlp24 directly contacts Bud20, and then intertwines around the Nog1-CTT, forming a Nog1-CTT:Rlp24 complex (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The last 40 residues of the Rlp24 C-terminal tail (155–190) recruit and activate the AAA-ATPase Drg1 to extract Rlp24 from the pre-60S.
source: The last 40 residues of the Rlp24 C-terminal tail (155–190), which remain unresolved in cryo-EM structures (Wu et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2019), recruit and activate the AAA-ATPase Drg1 to extract Rlp24 from the pre-60S (Pertschy et al., 2007; Lo et al., 2010; Kappel et al., 2012; Altvater et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rlp24-TAP did not mislocalize to the cytoplasm upon Nog1DN expression.
source: As judged by immunofluorescence, Rlp24-TAP did not mislocalize to the cytoplasm upon Nog1DN expression (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Nog1DN accumulation on a cytoplasmic pre-60S did not interfere with the release and recycling of Rlp24 back to the nucleus.
source: As judged by immunofluorescence, Rlp24-TAP did not mislocalize to the cytoplasm upon Nog1DN expression (Figure 4B), suggesting that Nog1DN accumulation on a cytoplasmic pre-60S did not interfere with the release and recycling of Rlp24 back to the nucleus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunofluorescence data.

claim: Drg1-ATPase activity is necessary and sufficient to release Rlp24 from the pre-60S.
source: This finding is in agreement with previous studies which showed that Drg1-ATPase activity is necessary and sufficient to release Rlp24 from the pre-60S (Kappel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The presence of Nog1DN on the pre-60S did not interfere with recruitment of r-protein eL24 (yeast Rpl24).
source: The presence of Nog1DN on the pre-60S did not interfere with recruitment of r-protein eL24 (yeast Rpl24), as judged by Western analyses (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The release of the Rlp24-interacting assembly factor Bud20 from the pre-60S is not impaired in Nog1DN-expressing cells.
source: Cell-biological studies indicate that the release of the Rlp24-interacting assembly factor Bud20 from the pre-60S is also not impaired in Nog1DN-expressing cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Nog1DN does not disturb initiation of the pre-60S cytoplasmic maturation cascade.
source: We conclude that Nog1DN does not disturb initiation of the pre-60S cytoplasmic maturation cascade.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The Lsg1-TAP:Drg1DN particle accumulated Rlp24, Drg1DN, Nog1 and another GTPase Nug1.
source: While the Lsg1-TAP:Drg1DN particle accumulated Rlp24, Drg1DN, Nog1 and another GTPase Nug1 (Altvater et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Lsg1-TAP:Nog1DN particle accumulated only Nog1DN, and not Rlp24, Drg1 or Nug1.
source: the Lsg1-TAP:Nog1DN particle accumulated only Nog1DN, and not Rlp24, Drg1 or Nug1 (Figure 3B and Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SWATH-MS analysis and fluorescence microscopy.

claim: Nog1DN eviction from the pre-60S occurs after Drg1-mediated Rlp24 release.
source: On the basis of these data, we conclude that Nog1DN eviction from the pre-60S occurs after Drg1-mediated Rlp24 release.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Lsg1-TAP:Nog1DN failed to recruit Yvh1 and accumulated Mrt4.
source: SWATH-MS and Western analyses revealed that Lsg1-TAP:Nog1DN failed to recruit Yvh1, and accumulated Mrt4 (Figure 3B and Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SWATH-MS and Western analyses shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Nog1DN-expressing cells mislocalized Mrt4-GFP into the cytoplasm.
source: In agreement with these data, we found that Nog1DN-expressing cells mislocalized Mrt4-GFP into the cytoplasm (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4C.

claim: uL10 recruitment to Lsg1-TAP:Nog1DN was impaired.
source: Accordingly, Western analyses showed that uL10 recruitment to Lsg1-TAP:Nog1DN was impaired (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The Yvh1-binding site on the pre-60S clashes with the Nog1-G domain.
source: Cryo-EM studies suggest that the Yvh1-binding site on the pre-60S clashes with the Nog1-G domain (Figure 4D) (Zhou et al., 2019; Kargas et al., 2019)
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 4D and cited work.

claim: Nog1 eviction is critical for stalk assembly.
source: Cryo-EM studies suggest that the Yvh1-binding site on the pre-60S clashes with the Nog1-G domain (Figure 4D) (Zhou et al., 2019; Kargas et al., 2019), providing an explanation as to why Nog1 eviction is critical for stalk assembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: Drg1DN-expressing cells are impaired in Mrt4 release and consequently stalk assembly.

claim: Stalk assembly requires Drg1-ATPase activity and a functional Nog1-GTPase domain.

claim: Nog1DN-expressing cells when treated with the Drg1-inhibitor diazaborine (DIA) mislocalized Arx1-GFP to the cytoplasm.

claim: Failure to insert Rei1-CTT into the PET by attaching a bulky domain (rei1-TAP) blocks Arx1 release and progression of cytoplasmic maturation.

claim: A Rlp24 mutant lacking Nog1-interacting helices, Rlp24∆91–105, impaired yeast growth in a dominant-negative manner.

claim: Rlp24∆91–105-expressing cells did not mislocalize Arx1-GFP, Mrt4-GFP and Tif6-GFP to the cytoplasm.
